lines.text: Vera, “dog bites man” or “man bites dog”. Same thing?
lines.say: Vera, dog bites man, or man bites dog. Same thing?

lines.text: Not to you. But attention alone treats the tokens as a set.
So if you shuffle us, nothing changes?
Every token computes the same result. So each token must be told where it sits.
Like a seat number? One, two, three?
The original transformer, in 2017, added a fixed pattern of sines and cosines.
lines.say: The original transformer, in twenty seventeen, added a fixed pattern of sines and cosines.

lines.text: Each row is one position. Each pair of columns is a wave with its own speed.
Fast waves on the left, slow ones on the right?
Yes. Fast ones tell neighbours apart, slow ones the rough place, like the hands of a clock.
Why waves, and not plain numbers?
Compare one position's pattern with every other. Neighbours come out most similar.
Move from position 20 to 45: the same shape, just shifted.
lines.say: Move from position twenty to forty-five: the same shape, just shifted.

lines.text: So it's how far apart we are, not where we are.
Do today's models still add waves?
Most use RoPE, from 2021. It rotates pairs of numbers in the query and the key.
lines.say: Most use rope, from twenty twenty-one. It rotates pairs of numbers in the query and the key.

lines.text: The angle grows with position: a fast pair, a medium pair, a slow pair.
And when two tokens compare notes?
Only the difference of their angles survives: relative distance, directly.
Does this matter for long documents?
Yes. Position is one of the pieces that had to be stretched to make very long contexts possible.
Can I play with the waves?
Drag the position slider in the Position chapter; Deep mode adds the circles.
Found my seat. Now I'm spinning.
